strapline: The government calls the third-term debate imaginary as a 25 November march is planned; the sedition case comes to Lusaka; Mandevu gets its MP; the Suns go to Nairobi

stories.title: 'An imaginary issue': the government asks civil society to rethink its 25 November term-limits march, as the Evangelical Fellowship demands that the debate end now
stories.excerpt: Twelve civil society organisations have notified the police of a procession on Wednesday 25 November in defence of the two-term presidential limit, and the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia has called for all talk of removing the limit to cease immediately. The Chief Government Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, replied on Thursday that every Zambian may hold an opinion but that an opinion is not a government decision, and asked the organisers why they would march against something that is not happening.

image.label: Two terms, one march
image.caption: Civil society groups plan a 25 November procession in defence of presidential term limits; the government says the debate is imaginary.

body: The argument over whether Zambia's presidents should remain limited to two terms has reached the point where the government is being asked to stop something it says is not happening. News Diggers reported on Friday 6 November that the Chief Government Spokesperson, Elvis Nkandu, had urged a consortium of civil society organisations to reconsider a procession planned for Wednesday 25 November, and had asked why anyone would protest against what he called an imaginary issue. In the same week the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia demanded that all discussion of removing presidential term limits stop at once.

body.text: Twelve organisations and a letter to the police

body: The procession was announced in a joint statement. Zambia Monitor reported on Thursday 5 November that the statement, headed "Joint CSO Statement on the Planned Peaceful Assembly in Defence of the Constitution and Presidential Term Limits", was signed by Josiah Kalala of the Chapter One Foundation, Leah Mitaba of the Zambia Council for Social Development and Maurice Nyambe of Transparency International Zambia, and that the organisers had notified the Zambia Police Service of a peaceful procession and public assembly on 25 November. News Diggers listed twelve member organisations, among them Caritas Zambia, ActionAid, the Council of Churches in Zambia, the Free Press Initiative, the Non-Governmental Gender Organisations' Coordinating Council, the Alliance for Community Action, the Advocates for Democratic Governance Foundation and the LCK Freedom Foundation. The Zambian Observer, which carried the announcement on Wednesday 4 November, said the statement had been issued on Tuesday 3 November.

What prompted it, according to both Zambia Monitor and the Observer, was a petition presented to the National Assembly on 27 October by a group of citizens asking, among other proposals, for presidential term limits to be abolished. The organisations said they disagreed with the petitioners but respected their right to be heard. They also pointed to last year's constitutional review process, in which, they said, the committees that consulted the public recommended keeping two terms of five years each.

body.text: If those voices mattered last year, they matter this year.
body.attribution: Joint statement by Chapter One Foundation, the Zambia Council for Social Development and Transparency International Zambia, as reported by Zambia Monitor on 5 November

body: The Observer quoted the statement's description of term limits as "an important safeguard against excessive concentration of political power" and its view that "protecting the Constitution is a collective responsibility shared by all Zambians". News Diggers reported that the procession follows an earlier march by youth-led civil society groups on the same question.

Mr Nkandu's response came in an interview on Thursday 5 November, reported by News Diggers the next morning. He said that "every Zambian has every right, their freedoms to express their opinion" and that "not even government can gag such an opinion", but argued that the views being expressed amounted to opinion rather than policy. "So it's just an opinion which does not culminate into government doing" anything, he said, in the part of his remarks visible before the newspaper's paywall, and he asked the organisers to rethink the protest. The government has not, in any of the reports read for this edition, published a bill or formal proposal to change the two-term rule.

The Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia's intervention came through its Executive Director, Reverend Allan Kasungami, in a statement reported by The Zambian Observer on Thursday 5 November. He called the debate "unnecessary" and said it "risks plunging the country into political instability", described the constitution as "the cornerstone of Zambia's democracy" which "should not be altered for political expediency", and said that "all discussions regarding the removal of presidential term limits should cease immediately". He invoked the Oasis Declaration of 2001, when churches and civil society groups combined to oppose a third-term bid, and said the country should be concentrating on the cost of living, national healing after a divisive election, and public services. The Council of Churches in Zambia, a separate body, is among the organisers of the 25 November procession.

body.title: Key dates
items: **27 October** — a citizens' petition to the National Assembly proposes abolishing presidential term limits, among other changes
**3 November** — twelve civil society organisations issue a joint statement and notify the police of a procession
**5 November** — the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia demands the debate end; Elvis Nkandu calls the issue imaginary
**25 November** — planned peaceful procession and public assembly

body.confirmed: A consortium of civil society organisations has notified the police of a 25 November procession in defence of presidential term limits (News Diggers, Zambia Monitor, The Zambian Observer). The Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia has called for the debate to cease (The Zambian Observer). Elvis Nkandu has asked the organisers to reconsider and called the issue imaginary (News Diggers). A petition to abolish term limits was presented to the National Assembly on 27 October (Zambia Monitor, The Zambian Observer).
body.unverified: None of the reports read names the petitioners of 27 October or says who, if anyone, in government or the ruling party supports their proposal. No bill or formal government proposal to amend the two-term rule has been published. The police response to the notification, and the route and assembly point of the procession, had not been reported at the time of writing.

stories.title: Back to Lusaka: Judge Musona moves the Mundubile–Zulu sedition case out of Solwezi, while the treason bail hearing for 18 accused is put back to Friday 6 November
stories.excerpt: Of the two decisions expected on Thursday 5 November in the cases of Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, one arrived and one did not. The Zambian Observer reports that High Court Judge Edward Musona, sitting in Solwezi, ordered the sedition case transferred to a subordinate court in Lusaka, where the two men live and were arrested. In Lusaka, the three-judge panel hearing their constitutional bail petition allowed the State to raise a fresh jurisdictional objection and adjourned to 09:00 on Friday.

image.label: Solwezi to Lusaka
image.caption: The sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu moves from Solwezi to Lusaka; their bail hearing resumes on Friday 6 November.

body: Thursday 5 November was meant to settle two questions for Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu: where they would answer sedition charges, and whether they and sixteen co-accused in a separate treason case would be released on constitutional bail. By the evening the first had an answer and the second had a new date.

The background was set out on Wednesday 4 November by the Times of Zambia and News Diggers. Lusaka High Court Judge Edward Musona, sitting in Solwezi, had heard a challenge to the authority of the Solwezi Magistrates' Court to try the two men, and the State's advocate had told the court the ruling would come at 14:00 on Thursday. News Diggers reported that the charges arise from Facebook posts of 14 August 2026, the day after the general election, in which Mr Mundubile allegedly said his party was leading according to its parallel vote tabulation and called on the Electoral Commission to resume counting, and that the defence argued the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka, where both men were at the time. The Times quoted defence lawyer Chifumu Banda welcoming the timetable: "This is good because we now know when the pending issue of jurisdiction will finally be determined by the court."

The Zambian Observer, citing court records, reported on Thursday that Justice Musona ordered the case moved to a subordinate court in Lusaka and granted leave to appeal. According to the Observer's account of the order, the judge relied on Section 80 of the Criminal Procedure Code and on three findings: that the two men reside in Lusaka, "a fact which was not disputed"; that they were arrested and have been held in custody in Lusaka; and that Lusaka is the more convenient and appropriate forum. A separate Observer report said the court found the Solwezi Subordinate Court "was not the correct and appropriate forum". The two men face two counts of seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code. The Observer said they had been travelling about 440 kilometres from Kabwe, where they are held, for each Solwezi hearing.

body.text: The respected Judge Musona's decision to move the case to a Lusaka subordinate court in my view is good for the State (DPP & AG).
body.attribution: Sakwiba Sikota, lead defence counsel for Brian Mundubile, in remarks reported by The Zambian Observer on 5 November

body: Mr Sikota argued, in the same report, that the State would no longer have to move lawyers and witnesses to Solwezi for every sitting, and asked that the two accused also be brought to Lusaka, which he said made "logistical, security and financial sense". No date for the first Lusaka hearing was given.

The constitutional bail petition by Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and sixteen others is before a three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court which Zambia Monitor identified on 29 October as Judges Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga. That day the panel fixed 09:00 on 5 November and warned, in the words of defence lawyer Milner Katolo quoted by the Monitor, that "this is the last adjournment". The Observer reported that when the matter was called on Thursday, under a heavy police presence around the court, the Acting Chief State Advocate, Chibesa Mulonda, argued that constitutional bail could not be pursued through a constitutional petition and that the applicants should seek bail in the criminal proceedings. Mr Katolo objected that the Director of Public Prosecutions was barred from raising the point after failing to file an answer to the petition. The court dismissed that objection, allowed the State to raise its jurisdictional challenge once it had filed a response, and adjourned to 09:00 on Friday 6 November.

The Observer also reported that Mr Zulu told the court he would represent himself and declined an adjournment to prepare, citing the 1975 case of Shamwana v The People, in which the accused likewise acted for himself. The eighteen have been in custody since 14 August and face treason and terrorism-related charges which carry life imprisonment on conviction. The State's affidavit opposing bail, reported by Zambia Monitor on 29 October and sworn by Senior Superintendent Donald Mulimba, argues that the two leaders are a flight risk, that their networks create a risk of interference with witnesses, and that "the balancing of interests test favours the State". Mr Mundubile has denied that his party had a militia and, according to the Monitor, has said it "did not support violence or attempts to overthrow the constitutional order".

body.confirmed: Judge Musona ordered the sedition case transferred from Solwezi to a subordinate court in Lusaka and granted leave to appeal (The Zambian Observer, citing court records; the ruling was scheduled for 5 November according to the Times of Zambia and News Diggers). The bail hearing was adjourned to 09:00 on Friday 6 November after the court allowed the State to raise a jurisdictional objection (The Zambian Observer). The panel had set 5 November as a final date (Zambia Monitor).
body.unverified: The date of the first Lusaka sitting of the sedition case, and whether the accused will be moved from Kabwe. Whether the State will appeal the transfer. The outcome of the jurisdictional argument on bail, which the court had not decided at the time of writing. No outlet other than The Zambian Observer had published a full account of Thursday's rulings in the pages read for this edition.

stories.title: Mandevu has an MP without a ballot: Adrian Banda is declared elected, a minister denies pushing out the Tonse candidate, and the ECZ says it counts votes, not makes them
stories.excerpt: The UPND's Adrian Banda was declared the winner of the Mandevu parliamentary by-election on Thursday 5 November without a vote being cast, The Zambian Observer reports, a week after his three opponents withdrew. Lusaka Province Minister Obvious Mwaliteta has denied Tonse Alliance claims that he warned the FDD's Daniel Chisenga he would 'get into trouble', and ECZ commissioner McDonald Chipenzi told agents in Sioma that the Commission counts votes and does not manufacture them.

image.label: Declared, not elected
image.caption: Adrian Banda of the UPND is declared Mandevu's MP after all three rivals withdrew; a minister denies pressuring one of them.

body: Mandevu's parliamentary by-election ended on Thursday 5 November the way the Electoral Commission of Zambia said it would: with a declaration and no poll. The Zambian Observer reported celebrations in the constituency as Adrian Banda of the United Party for National Development was declared the winner, the only candidate left after the Forum for Democracy and Development's Daniel Chisenga, the Leadership Movement's Ntazana Musukuma Mutungwa and the independent Daniel Daka pulled out. The Observer's short report did not name the declaring officer.

The legal route had been laid out a week earlier. Zambia Monitor reported on Friday 30 October that the Commission's Chief Electoral Officer, Brown Kasaro, had issued a public notice citing Regulations 20(3) and 52(2) of the Electoral Process (General) Regulations of 2016, after receiving three withdrawal letters dated 28 October, and had said Mr Banda, "being the only validly nominated candidate, will be declared duly elected Member of Parliament". The Zambia Daily Mail repeated on Thursday morning that the seat would be filled without a poll. Mr Banda stood in Mandevu as an independent in August; the Observer reported on 1 October, carrying a UPND media release, that he had rejoined the ruling party, saying, "I have rejoined the UPND because it is a winning team."

The withdrawals remain contested. News Diggers reported on Thursday that the Tonse Alliance's secretary general, Muhabi Lungu, had claimed Lusaka Province Minister Obvious Mwaliteta telephoned Mr Chisenga and warned him he would "get into trouble". Mr Mwaliteta, in an interview on Wednesday 4 November, denied it. "I cannot entice people to withdraw," he said, describing himself as a politician who believes in democracy and saying he lacked the capacity to do what Mr Lungu alleged. He told Mr Lungu to put his own house in order and said, according to the newspaper, that the alliance had lacked the money to back its candidate. The rest of his remarks sit behind the newspaper's paywall, and Mr Chisenga's own account of why he withdrew has not appeared in the reports read for this edition.

The Zambia Daily Mail reported on Thursday morning that President Hakainde Hichilema was expected in Mandevu that day, at the Mutambe Community grounds, to meet residents and take their questions, following a State House announcement which the paper said had drawn more than 13,000 comments within three hours. The Zambian Observer had reported on Wednesday that the President framed the visit as an unscripted engagement, telling residents, "bring your neighbours, bring your questions and let us talk about what matters to you", and that fuel prices, inflation and jobs were expected to dominate. No account of what was said at the meeting was available in the pages read for this edition.

Thursday was also polling day in six council wards. Ahead of the Mbeta ward poll in Sioma, Western Province, ECZ commissioner McDonald Chipenzi told a stakeholders' briefing on Tuesday 3 November, reported by the Zambia Daily Mail and News Diggers, that parties should recruit honest polling agents for every station rather than blame the Commission afterwards. "Our role as a commission is to count votes, and not to manufacture votes. We don't manufacture votes. We only want counts," he said, according to the Daily Mail. News Diggers quoted him saying preparations had concluded and "we're ready for the polls". Results from the six wards had not been published in the sources read at the time of writing.

stories.title: 'We don't arrest on rumours': the ACC says it is investigating seven Auditor General queries and six FIC referrals, as suspected illicit flows fall to US$1.8 billion
stories.excerpt: The Anti-Corruption Commission's Director General, Daphne Pauline Soko Chabu, says the Commission is investigating seven complaints from the 2025 Auditor General's report and six cases referred by the Financial Intelligence Centre, one of which, over K2 million meant for school feeding, has already produced five arrests. She also noted that suspected illicit financial flows fell from US$3.5 billion in 2024 to US$1.8 billion in 2025, and that an audit query is not in itself proof of corruption.

image.label: Seven and six
image.caption: The Anti-Corruption Commission says it is investigating seven Auditor General queries and six FIC referrals from 2025.

body: The Anti-Corruption Commission has set out what it is doing with the two documents that dominated last week's conversation about public money, the 2025 Auditor General's report and the Financial Intelligence Centre's 2025 Trends Report. In a statement issued in Lusaka on Wednesday 4 November, reported by Zambia Monitor that afternoon and described by News Diggers on Thursday as a press briefing, the Director General, Daphne Pauline Soko Chabu, said the Commission is investigating seven corruption-related complaints arising from the audit report and six cases referred to it by the FIC in 2025.

Of the six FIC referrals, one has been concluded. According to Zambia Monitor, it involved more than K2 million intended for the school feeding programme and led to the arrest of five people, including the Chama District Board Secretary and bank officials; the other five remain under investigation. News Diggers put the same case at over K2 million and five arrests. Lusaka Brief has not seen the charge sheets and does not name the accused.

The Director General drew attention to two falling numbers. Zambia Monitor reported her saying that unresolved audit findings dropped from 33 in 2024 to 27 at the end of the 2025 audits, which she called "an encouraging development", and that suspected illicit financial flows fell from US$3.5 billion in 2024 to US$1.8 billion in 2025. News Diggers reported that she nonetheless regarded US$1.8 billion as still a great deal of money.

body.text: A query is not a charge

body: Much of the statement, as both outlets reported it, was about process. She said audit queries and irregularities do not automatically amount to corruption, though they can signal weaknesses that lead to abuse of office or misappropriation, and that being named in an audit or FIC report does not make a person guilty. News Diggers summarised her position in its headline: the Commission does not arrest on rumours, but "first conducts investigations and only takes action after gathering evidence". Zambia Monitor quoted her saying that "the Commission is required to conduct thorough investigations, establish the facts and gather sufficient evidence" before acting, and that earlier FIC-linked investigations have already led to arrests and prosecutions.

The statement follows the FIC's own account, carried in Lusaka Brief this week, of a K1 billion mineral smuggling syndicate and a company that functioned as a payment channel for K222 million and US$5.7 million in three months. The Commission did not say whether either of those case studies is among the six referrals.

stories.title: Fourteen thousand stalls, 405 allocated: Sialubalo tells councils to move street vendors with dignity and hand out market spaces fairly, a month into Operation Clear Path
stories.excerpt: Lusaka City Council has more than 14,000 trading spaces in 34 markets available for immediate allocation but has handed out only 405 of them, the Minister of Local Government and Rural Development, Gift Sialubalo, told Parliament in a ministerial statement on Tuesday 3 November. With about 8,000 registered street vendors in the city, he said the arithmetic allows every one of them a stall, and told councils that enforcement must be lawful and humane and that allocation must be transparent.

image.label: 14,000 spaces, 405 taken
image.caption: The local government minister says Lusaka has 14,000 market spaces for 8,000 registered street vendors, but only 405 have been allocated.

body: A month after Lusaka City Council began clearing traders from the capital's streets, the minister responsible has told Parliament that the problem is no longer a shortage of market stalls but the way they are handed out. The Zambia Daily Mail reported on Wednesday 4 November, and News Diggers on Thursday, that the Minister of Local Government and Rural Development, Gift Sialubalo, had given a ministerial statement on street-vending control and the allocation of trading spaces on Tuesday 3 November.

His figures, as reported by both outlets, were these: Lusaka has 34 markets with more than 14,000 trading spaces available for immediate allocation; only 405 have so far been allocated; and the city has roughly 8,000 registered street vendors, all of whom could be accommodated in the space available. News Diggers added that Operation Clear Path, the council's campaign to remove vendors from the central business district, was launched on 2 October, and that the council has introduced regular patrols to stop traders returning.

The Daily Mail reported that Mr Sialubalo cited allegations of unfair allocation, multiple occupation of trading spaces by single traders, unauthorised subletting and demands for unofficial payments, and that he urged local authorities to allocate stalls "in a transparent, fair and accountable manner". He said removing traders without offering alternative spaces might not solve street vending. News Diggers reported that he asked councils to inform traders of the spaces available to them.

On enforcement, the minister's language was pointed. The Daily Mail quoted him saying it should be carried out "lawfully, professionally, consistently and humanely"; News Diggers headlined the same message as an instruction to evict vendors with dignity and to ensure enforcement officers treat them accordingly. The newspaper's report quotes him beginning a passage on the capital's role as "the country's principal commercial" centre, but the rest sits behind its paywall.

The statement is the clearest official account yet of the gap between the council's clearance campaign and the alternative it is supposed to offer. Lusaka Brief has reported since early October on the dawn operations, the fines handed down by a fast-track court and the second phase of the operation in Katondo Street; the minister's numbers suggest that, five weeks in, about one in twenty of the city's registered vendors has been given a market space.

stories.title: Paid in advance, never delivered: the ZPPA bars two suppliers of school laboratory and home economics equipment from public tenders for a year over World Bank-funded contracts
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Public Procurement Authority has suspended Biogenix Limited and Leisely Howards Limited from public procurement for one year each after investigating complaints from the Ministry of Education under the World Bank-funded Zambia Education Enhancement Project. Biogenix took a K239,494 advance to supply laboratory equipment to 82 secondary schools and did not deliver; Leisely Howards received a 25 per cent advance on a K8.62 million home economics contract and made late deliveries the ministry rejected.

image.label: Two suspensions
image.caption: The procurement authority has barred two firms from public tenders for a year over undelivered school equipment contracts.

body: Two companies that took advance payments to equip Zambian secondary schools and did not deliver have been barred from public procurement for a year. Zambia Monitor reported on Wednesday 4 November, and News Diggers on Thursday 5 November, that the Zambia Public Procurement Authority had suspended Biogenix Limited and Leisely Howards Limited following investigations it opened in September. The Authority's Assistant Public Relations Officer, Lucy Lumbe, announced the decisions in a statement in Lusaka on Wednesday.

Both contracts were awarded by the Ministry of Education under the Zambia Education Enhancement Project, which is financed by the World Bank. Biogenix Limited was contracted to supply and deliver laboratory equipment and reagents to 82 secondary schools and, according to both outlets, received an advance payment of K239,494. Zambia Monitor reported the Authority's finding that the firm "did not deliver the goods during the contract period", that the case began with a complaint from the ministry, and that the suspension took effect on 23 October 2026 under sections 95(1) and 96(g) of the Public Procurement Act No. 8 of 2020.

body.text: A second suspension on top of a first

body: Leisely Howards Limited's contract, for home economics equipment for schools under the same project, was worth K8.62 million, or US$332,791.54, and was awarded in December 2024, Zambia Monitor reported. The firm received a 25 per cent advance of K2.16 million that month and was to deliver within 12 to 16 weeks. It made partial deliveries in June and July 2025, after the contract had expired, and the ministry rejected the items because they did not meet specifications. The company was already serving a one-year suspension from a separate tender, due to end on 22 January 2027; the Monitor quoted the Authority's statement that it "has suspended Leisely Howards Limited from participating in public procurement, effective 22nd January 2027", so the new ban begins when the old one ends. News Diggers put the combined value of the contracts and payments at issue at K8.8 million.

Zambia Monitor reported that the Authority acted under Section 6(h) of the Public Procurement Act, which requires it to investigate and act on complaints from procuring entities, bidders, suppliers or the public. Neither report carried a response from either company, and only the excerpts of the ZPPA statement published by the two outlets were available. The suspensions are administrative sanctions by a regulator; neither report mentions criminal proceedings.
The decisions come in a week in which the Anti-Corruption Commission said it is investigating a separate case involving more than K2 million of school feeding money.

stories.title: US$240 million of US$1.52 billion: the Rural Electrification Authority tells the Livingstone summit how far it has got with the master plan for universal access by 2030
stories.excerpt: Zambia has so far mobilised US$240 million from the government and the World Bank towards the US$1.52 billion its updated Rural Electrification Master Plan says is needed to reach universal electricity access by 2030, the Rural Electrification Authority's chief executive, Alex Mbumba, told a panel at the Zimbabwe-Zambia Energy Projects Summit in Livingstone, according to News Diggers. The plan, launched in April, relies on solar mini-grids and home systems as well as grid extension.

image.label: US$240m of US$1.52bn
image.caption: The Rural Electrification Authority says US$240 million has been raised towards a US$1.52 billion plan for universal access by 2030.

body: The third Zimbabwe-Zambia Energy Projects Summit in Livingstone, which Lusaka Brief reported on Thursday as it opened, has produced a figure for how far Zambia's rural electrification plan has got. News Diggers reported on Thursday 5 November that the Rural Electrification Authority's Chief Executive Officer, Alex Mbumba, told a panel discussion entitled "Rural Power Play: Turning Access into Productive Use" that US$240 million had been mobilised from the government and the World Bank towards the plan.

That is against a total requirement which Mr Mbumba put at US$1.52 billion. "If you read the Electrification Master Plan, you will see that it provides an envelope of US$1.52 billion required," he said, in the part of his remarks published before the newspaper's paywall. He said the plan aims to deliver connections through grid extension, solar mini-grids and solar home systems, and would bridge the gap between the private and public sectors. The rest of his contribution was not available.

The updated Rural Electrification Master Plan was launched in April at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre by the Minister of Energy, Makozo Chikote, the trade publication SolarQuarter reported on 15 April 2026. Its target is universal electricity access by 2030, in line with Vision 2030, and its cost was put at about US$1.52 billion, the same figure Mr Mbumba quoted in Livingstone. SolarQuarter reported that the minister described the plan as "bankable", that it replaces scattered projects with a coordinated programme meant to avoid duplication, that the Authority is shifting its focus to "last mile" connections for remote communities, and that a digital platform for the public to track progress was promised by the end of 2026.

On the summit's own figures, as Lusaka Brief reported on Thursday, Zimbabwe's ZESA counted 635 megawatts of generation under construction while ZESCO described a market opening to private producers. Mr Mbumba's numbers show the scale of the rural task on the Zambian side: with roughly a sixth of the money in hand and a little over four years to the 2030 target, the remainder depends on the public-private partnerships the plan was built to attract. Neither report gives a connection count achieved so far under the updated plan.

stories.title: Five from five: Munali Suns finish Group E unbeaten with an 80–60 win over Soweto Panthers and head for the Elite 16 in Nairobi from 23 November
stories.excerpt: Munali Suns completed a perfect Road to BAL 2027 group stage at NASDEC in Lusaka, beating South Africa's Soweto Panthers 80–60 in their final Group E game, News Diggers reports, two days after holding off Harare Kings 70–69. The Times of Zambia reports that the Elite 16 East Division will be played in Nairobi from 23 to 29 November, and coach Michael Mai says planning is under way to have all his players cleared for it.

image.label: Five from five
image.caption: Munali Suns finished the Road to BAL Group E stage unbeaten and go to the Elite 16 in Nairobi from 23 to 29 November.

body: Five games, five wins, and a place in the Elite 16 secured with a match to spare and then sealed in style: Munali Suns have finished their Road to BAL 2027 group exactly as they would have drawn it. News Diggers reported on Thursday 5 November that the Suns beat South Africa's Soweto Panthers 80–60 at the NASDEC Sports Complex in their final Group E fixture, finishing the group with what the paper called a flawless record. The report said the Suns led 21–13 at the end of the first quarter and 26–18 early in the second, and named Jared Mweetwa as the standout, though the rest of the scoring is behind the newspaper's paywall.

The qualification had been confirmed two nights earlier. The Times of Zambia reported on Wednesday 4 November that the Suns beat Zimbabwe's Harare Kings 70–69, leading 38–25 at half time and 58–40 after three quarters before the Kings outscored them 29–12 in the fourth and closed to a single point. Ofuya Djaduighe scored 20 points, Douglas Kandulu pulled down 20 rebounds, eight of them offensive, and Frank Sianne, Wamundu Simwinga and Christopher Carter added 11, 11 and 10. Munashe Makunde led the Kings with 19 and Emmanuel Muteba Shine had 17.

The Times reported that the top two in the group advance to the Elite 16 East Division, to be played in Nairobi, Kenya, from 23 to 29 November. In the other Group E games it reported, Mozambique's Ferroviario da Beira beat Malawi's Bravehearts 110–81, with Ismael Nunamade scoring 27, and Botswana's Dolphins beat Soweto Panthers 63–56, Dallan Coleman scoring 30 with seven three-pointers.

body.text: It's about hard work. Hard work and teamwork…that's everything.
body.attribution: Michael Mai, Munali Suns head coach, in a post-match interview after the win over Harare Kings, as reported by the Times of Zambia on 4 November

body: Mr Mai told the Times that the team had been preaching the same message since the first game, that "everything is about preparation", and that financial support had been the single biggest help in getting Zambia ready for the Elite 16. "Planning is underway and we are hoping to have all the players cleared," he said. He also thanked the supporters who filled NASDEC through the week.

The Suns' run through the group went: 79–66 over Bravehearts, 87–85 over Ferroviario da Beira, 96–56 over Dolphins, 70–69 over Harare Kings and 80–60 over Soweto Panthers, as reported by News Diggers and the Times of Zambia across the week. Lusaka Brief has followed each game since the opening win over Bravehearts.

stories.title: Third year on the list: Barbra Banda is shortlisted for the FIFPRO Women's World 11 again, with the final team to be announced on Monday 9 November
stories.excerpt: Barbra Banda is one of 26 players, and one of eight forwards, on the shortlist for the 2026 FIFPRO Women's World 11, the players' union announced, placing the Copper Queens forward alongside Alexia Putellas, Aitana Bonmatí and Ada Hegerberg. The Times of Zambia reports it is her third successive nomination after she made the team in 2024 and 2025. The final eleven, chosen by 26,317 professional footballers from 75 countries, will be revealed on Monday 9 November.

image.label: 26 names, one Zambian
image.caption: Barbra Banda is on the 26-player shortlist for the 2026 FIFPRO Women's World 11, to be announced on 9 November.

body: Days after her nomination for the CAF Women's Player of the Year, Barbra Banda has another shortlist to her name. The Times of Zambia reported on Thursday 5 November that the Orlando Pride and Zambia forward is among the 26 players shortlisted for the 2026 FIFPRO Women's World 11, the team of the year chosen by professional footballers themselves. FIFPRO's own announcement, published on 2 November, lists her among eight forwards with Chelsea's Aggie Beever-Jones, Real Madrid's Athenea del Castillo, OL Lyonnes' Ada Hegerberg, Arsenal's Chloe Kelly and Alessia Russo, and Barcelona's Ewa Pajor and Claudia Pina.

The shortlist, FIFPRO said, reflects the votes of 26,317 professional footballers from 75 countries for performances between August 2025 and August 2026, with the men's and women's teams of the year voted on together. It is made up of three goalkeepers, eight defenders, seven midfielders and eight forwards. The Times listed Ann-Katrin Berger, Catalina Coll and Hannah Hampton in goal; Ona Batlle, Mapi León, Irene Paredes, Lucy Bronze, Ellie Carpenter, Emily Fox, Alex Greenwood and Katie McCabe in defence; and Aitana Bonmatí, Patri Guijarro, Alexia Putellas, Vicky López, Ella Toone, Aneale Le Moguedec and Morocco's Ghizlane Chebbak in midfield.

The Times of Zambia reported that this is Ms Banda's third FIFPRO nomination and that she made the final eleven in each of the two previous editions, 2024 and 2025. The newspaper described her as the only African player to have been named to the World 11 in those years. Ms Chebbak's presence on this year's shortlist means she is not the only African in contention this time.

FIFPRO said the final World 11 will be announced on Monday 9 November from 14:00 Central European Time, which is 15:00 in Lusaka, on its digital platforms. The CAF award for which Ms Banda is also shortlisted, alongside goalkeeper Hazel Nali in the Goalkeeper of the Year category, is decided in Lagos on 7 December, as Lusaka Brief reported on Thursday.
Neither the Times of Zambia report nor FIFPRO's announcement carries a comment from Ms Banda, the Football Association of Zambia or her club.

stories.title: Nkana go top of Stream A, ten-man Zanaco throw away a lead against MUZA, and Nkwazi end Red Arrows' 19-month unbeaten home run before the international break
stories.excerpt: The midweek round of the transitional MTN Super League sent Nkana to the top of Stream A on 13 points after Charles Zulu's goal beat Kansanshi Dynamos 1–0 in Kitwe, ZamFoot reports, while Zanaco, reduced to ten men when goalkeeper Francis Mwansa was sent off, led FC MUZA before Lewis Kasono's 93rd-minute equaliser made it 2–2 at Sunset Stadium. At Nkoloma, News Diggers reports, George Ndhlovu's lob gave Nkwazi a 1–0 win and Red Arrows their first home defeat since 9 April 2025.

image.label: Midweek in Stream A
image.caption: Nkana lead Stream A after beating Kansanshi; Zanaco drew 2–2 with MUZA; Nkwazi ended Red Arrows' long home run.

body: The Super League went into its November international break with a new leader in Stream A and the end of one of the longest home records in the country. ZamFoot reported on Thursday 5 November that Nkana beat Kansanshi Dynamos 1–0 at Nkana Stadium in Kitwe on Wednesday, Charles Zulu scoring in the 53rd minute, to move to the top of Stream A with 13 points from six matches, keep an unbeaten home record in the transitional campaign and end a two-match run without a goal.

body.text: It was a tactical game. He knows me and he knows my tricks.
body.attribution: Elijah Tana, Nkana head coach, on opposing coach Denis Makinka after the win over Kansanshi Dynamos, as reported by ZamFoot on 5 November

body: Mr Tana praised Mr Makinka as tactically astute and said Kansanshi had made it hard for his side to impose themselves, but was less pleased with striker Lazarus Kambole, who he said "was not up to the grade where I know him". "For this year, we want to do something good for Nkana," he said. Nkana's next match is away to FC MUZA in Mazabuka.

MUZA go into that game second in Stream A on 12 points and still unbeaten, after a 2–2 draw with Zanaco at Sunset Stadium on Wednesday. ZamFoot reported that Kiala Wa Kiala and Tobias Chungu put MUZA two up by the 30th minute, that Dominic Kanda pulled one back in the 57th and that Zanaco then went ahead despite having goalkeeper Francis Mwansa sent off, only for Lewis Kasono to equalise three minutes into stoppage time. Zanaco sit fourth on 11 points. Their assistant coach, Noel Mwandila, told ZamFoot it had been "a tough game, especially after the red card" and that "football is about concentration until the last whistle"; the next fixture is against the champions, Power Dynamos.

News Diggers reported on Thursday that Nkwazi beat Red Arrows 1–0 at Nkoloma Stadium, George Ndhlovu lobbing the goalkeeper in the 32nd minute after collecting an Andrew Mwape cross. The paper described it as a major upset: Arrows' first home defeat since 9 April 2025, ending a run of nineteen months unbeaten at the ground. Brian Chilimina had tested the Nkwazi goalkeeper early, and Arrows lost Ackim Mumba to injury in the 20th minute, Joseph Phiri replacing him. The remainder of the match report is behind the newspaper's paywall.

The league now pauses for the Chipolopolo's AFCON 2027 qualifiers against Burundi on 13 and 17 November, for which George Lwandamina named a 30-man provisional squad this week, as Lusaka Brief reported on Thursday.

analysis.title: Budget day: four things to read for in Musokotwane's speech
analysis.body: The 2027 budget reaches the National Assembly on Friday 6 November, a week later than first planned after the Vice-President moved the date because, as News Diggers reported, the government was still working on it. Four things will show what kind of budget it is. First, the Food Reserve Agency: the minister has said the agency should fund next year's purchases from maize sales, so a small Treasury line for the FRA would confirm that the K14.7 billion in farmer arrears was a one-off. Second, the borrowing mix: the second supplementary budget leaned on K18 billion of domestic borrowing, and Moody's upgrade to Caa1 this week will be tested by whether the 2027 financing plan keeps to the concessional-first line the minister set out. Third, the cost of five new ministries, which the minister says can be absorbed without new recruitment. Fourth, fuel: the US$200 million relief has ended and pump prices have risen, so any new levy or subsidy will be read closely. What the speech cannot settle is the drought the government says it is already paying to pre-empt; the numbers on Friday are a bet on next year's rains.

analysis.title: Imaginary or not, the term-limits argument is now about who moves first
analysis.body: The government's position on term limits is that there is nothing to discuss: a petition is an opinion, not a policy, and no bill exists. That is accurate as far as the public record goes, and it is why Elvis Nkandu can call the 25 November procession a protest against an imaginary issue. The organisers' position is also coherent: in 2001 the Oasis Declaration opposed a third term before any bill was tabled, and the two-term limit was examined by last year's review committees and retained, so waiting for a draft amendment would mean arguing after the decision is made. The two sides are not disputing facts so much as timing. For the government the question is whether a firm statement that it has no plan to touch Article 106 would end the matter, or would be read as a concession that a plan was considered. For the civil society groups the question is what a march achieves against a proposal nobody in authority has owned. What to watch: whether the police respond to the notification, whether any minister or ruling party official endorses or disowns the 27 October petition by name, and whether the Law Association answers the letter it was sent this week.

analysis.title: What moves with the sedition case, and what Friday's bail argument turns on
analysis.body: Judge Musona's order changes the geography of the Mundubile and Zulu cases but not their substance. The sedition charges, two counts under Section 57 of the Penal Code over Facebook posts of 14 August, now go to a subordinate court in Lusaka, where the accused live and were arrested; the defence has said the move suits the State as much as the accused, since witnesses and lawyers no longer travel to Solwezi. Leave to appeal was granted, so the State could still contest the venue. The bail petition is a different matter and the harder one. Thursday's hearing turned not on whether the eighteen should be released but on whether the High Court, sitting on a constitutional petition, can grant bail at all; the State says that belongs in the criminal courts. If the panel agrees, the application fails without the merits being heard and the accused, in custody since 14 August, would have to start again before the trial court. If it disagrees, the arguments about flight risk, witness interference and the length of detention without trial are finally reached. The panel said on 29 October that there would be no more adjournments. Friday at 09:00 is the test of that.
